before.title: 5-Speed Automatic Transmission Limp Mode / Valve Body Faults
before.description: The automatic 9-5 can drop into limp mode (locked in a single gear until restart) and develop slipping or harsh shifts. Early versions of the 5-speed automatic introduced around 2002 had valve-body and software issues; common triggers include the torque-converter lock-up solenoid, speed-sensor faults, and degraded fluid. In limp mode the car launches in a high gear with an unlocked converter and bangs into gear on upshifts.
before.solution: Diagnose for solenoid/speed-sensor codes; a revised valve body (2003+ units are far more durable) or solenoid replacement often resolves it. Critically, change to synthetic ATF every 50,000-60,000 miles to prevent recurrence.

proposal.title: 5-Speed Automatic Transmission Limp Mode / Valve Body Faults
proposal.description: Saab WIS identifies the AF33-5 five-speed automatic for the 2002 9-5 and explains that limp-home follows a sufficiently serious system fault, stores a DTC and leaves the gearbox under hydraulic control. That evidence does not prove that valve-body failure is the cause across every 2002-2009 car. WIS documents multiple electrical, hydraulic and mechanical faults that can request limp-home, so the frozen valve-body/software/solenoid/fluid composite and its claim that 2003-and-later units are more durable exceed the captured evidence.

Preserve the CHECK GEARBOX message and all TCM DTCs, confirm the exact gearbox, inspect wiring, power, fluid level and condition, and follow the DTC-specific WIS path before opening the valve body or condemning the transmission. Do not buy a valve body, solenoid, speed sensor, torque converter or ATF from this page; gearbox identity, DTC, fluid specification and root cause require VIN-level diagnosis.

before.title: 9-5 B235 Turbo Oil Sludge — Class Action Settlement
before.description: Early 2.3L B235 turbo Saab 9-5 (1999-2003 most affected) had an oil-sludge issue serious enough to trigger a class-action lawsuit and warranty extension. Root cause: undersized oil sump + tight PCV system + factory-recommended 10,000-mile oil change intervals combined to coke oil in the turbo oil-feed line. Many engines failed with seized turbos or spun bearings.
before.solution: Strict 3,000-5,000 mile oil intervals with full-synthetic 5W-30 (or 5W-40 for high-mileage) — Mobil 1 or Amsoil. Sludge-removal cycle (BG EPR, Liqui Moly Pro-Line) over multiple oil changes. Inspect the oil pickup screen if sump removed — heavy sludge means engine rebuild ($3,000-$5,000). Original class-action coverage long-expired.
affectedSystems: lubrication
turbocharger

before.title: Crankshaft Position Sensor (CPS) Hot No-Start
before.description: The crankshaft position sensor on the first-generation 9-5 (B235 engine) is a very common failure item. As it degrades it tends to fail when the engine is hot, producing the classic 'hot no-start': the engine cranks but will not fire when warm, then restarts after cooling. It can also cause intermittent stalling while driving, a real safety concern.
before.solution: Replace the crankshaft position sensor with an OEM/Bosch-quality part - cheap unbranded aftermarket sensors are reported to fail again within months. The sensor is relatively inexpensive but located awkwardly near the bell-housing.
symptoms: Hot no-start (cranks but won't start when warm)

proposal.title: Crankshaft Position Sensor (CPS) Hot No-Start
proposal.description: Saab WIS confirms that the Trionic T7 four-cylinder system depends on an inductive crankshaft-position sensor, can set P0336 or P0337, and has no substitute value for that sensor. The captured manufacturer material does not establish a heat-induced recurring failure, an all-1999-2009 incidence rate or the frozen all-engine scope. A hot crank/no-start or stall can also arise from fuel pressure, ignition, power, wiring, immobilizer, mechanical timing or another sensor and must be diagnosed from signals and DTCs.
proposal.solution: Preserve DTCs and reproduce the condition safely. During cranking, verify engine-speed data and the crank-sensor signal with the WIS test while also checking battery voltage, fuel pressure, ignition and wiring; compare hot and cold results before replacing the sensor. A stall in traffic or repeated no-start warrants professional diagnosis and towing as appropriate. Do not buy a crankshaft sensor from this page; engine, connector, signal test, VIN and exact failure path require confirmation.

Loss of crank-position tracking with P0336
Intermittent stall or restart complaint requiring parallel fuel and ignition checks

before.title: Direct Ignition Cassette (DIC) Failure
before.description: The Direct Ignition Cassette, which sits directly on top of the spark plugs and combines the coils into one unit, is a frequent failure point on the four-cylinder cars. Underhood heat and valve-cover gasket oil leaks contaminating the coil pack degrade the cassette over time, causing misfires, rough idle, hard starting and stalling. A failed cassette typically has a burnt smell and discoloration around the plug boots.
before.solution: Replace the Direct Ignition Cassette (use a quality OEM-grade unit) and renew the spark plugs at the same time, applying the correct Saab dielectric plug. Fixing any valve-cover gasket leak prevents repeat failures.

before.title: Engine Oil Sludge in 2.0T/2.3T Four-Cylinder
before.description: The B205/B235 four-cylinder turbo engines are notoriously prone to oil sludge buildup that clogs the fine oil-pickup screen in the sump, starving the engine of oil and leading to bearing or turbo failure. Contributing factors include an undersized/overworked PCV crankcase ventilation system, a catalytic converter mounted close to the oil pan that cooks the oil, and Saab's original long oil-change recommendation using conventional oil. Once the pickup screen is choked, oil pressure collapses and catastrophic engine damage follows.
before.solution: Install the updated PCV #6 breather kit, switch to full synthetic oil with short 3,000-5,000 mile change intervals, and if sludge is suspected drop the sump and clean it (including the oil-pickup screen) thoroughly. Severe cases require engine rebuild or replacement.

before.title: Fuel Line Leak from Damaged Pump Retaining Tabs - NHTSA Recall 07V087
before.description: On certain 2001-2005 9-5s, the retaining tabs that hold the fuel lines to the in-tank fuel pump can be damaged during production. Over time the fuel lines can loosen from the pump, allowing fuel to leak. With an ignition source present this leakage creates a fire risk. NHTSA recall 07V087000 covered roughly 94,000 9-3/9-5 vehicles.
before.solution: The dealer installs a bracket that secures the fuel lines to the fuel pump, free of charge under the recall. Owners should verify the recall was completed via their VIN.

A connection can loosen and leak fuel, creating a fire risk in the presence of an ignition source. Applicability and completion are VIN-specific; the combined campaign population must not be presented as a 9-5 owner-report count.

Check the VIN at NHTSA or with an authorized service provider. For an open campaign 07V087, the recall remedy is installation of the specified retaining bracket at no charge; do not improvise a clamp or disturb a leaking connection. Do not buy a fuel pump, line, seal or bracket from this page; recall completion and the exact remedy must be confirmed by VIN.

before.title: SID Display Dead/Missing Pixels
before.description: The Saab Information Display (SID) and the automatic climate control display almost universally develop missing or fading pixels as the cars age, making the clock, trip computer, radio and ACC readouts hard or impossible to read. The root cause is the ribbon cable connecting the LCD to its circuit board: the silver conductive traces become brittle and flake off, breaking the connection to rows of pixels.
before.solution: Replace the LCD ribbon cable (cheap DIY kits exist, no soldering needed) or fit a replacement LCD module. Professional pixel-repair services are also available. The unit itself usually does not need full replacement.

before.title: Takata Driver Airbag Inflator Rupture - NHTSA Recall 16E005 / 16V063
before.description: Second-generation 2010-2011 9-5 models (and 2003-2011 9-3s) use Takata PSDI-5 driver-airbag inflators that can degrade over time. Long-term moisture exposure can cause the propellant to burn too aggressively, over-pressurizing and rupturing the metal inflator body during deployment. Ruptured inflators can spray metal fragments into the cabin, causing serious injury or death.
before.solution: Have the dealer replace the driver airbag inflator under the Takata recall, free of charge. Owners should check VIN status, as parts availability was delayed in early notifications.

proposal.title: Takata Driver Airbag Inflator Rupture - NHTSA Recall 16E005 / 16V063
proposal.description: Campaign 16V063 was initially described with 2010-2011 Saab 9-5 vehicles, but the amended NHTSA campaign material and vehicle list identify 2006-2009 Saab 9-5 vehicles and state that 2010-2011 Saab 9-5 vehicles were removed. The current record therefore does not support the frozen identity as a currently applicable 2010-2011 recall or a promise of a free 16V063 remedy for those indexed years. A VIN lookup remains necessary because campaign history, market and prior repairs can differ.
proposal.solution: Do not disturb any airbag component. Check the VIN at NHTSA and with an authorized GM/Saab service contact for every open safety campaign and follow the current campaign instructions shown for that VIN. If the airbag warning lamp is on, have the supplemental-restraint system diagnosed by a qualified professional. Do not buy an inflator, driver airbag module or used steering-wheel airbag from this page; the frozen campaign-to-year match is contradicted and airbag service is VIN-controlled.

before.title: V6 Ignition Discharge Module (IGBT) Overheating - NHTSA Recall 05V399/06V410
before.description: On 6-cylinder gasoline 9-5s (B308 V6), the isolated gated bipolar transistor (IGBT) inside the ignition discharge module is overly susceptible to electrical loads and can overheat and burn out, most often at engine start-up. This causes the engine to stall, which could result in a crash. NHTSA issued recalls (05V399 for 2001 six-cylinders, and a related campaign covering 2002-2003 V6 units) requiring inspection and replacement of pre-January-2003 module versions.
before.solution: Have the recall performed at a dealer - they inspect the IDM version and replace any module built before January 2003 free of charge. Out of warranty, replace the ignition discharge module with the updated revision.

proposal.title: V6 Ignition Discharge Module (IGBT) Overheating - NHTSA Recall 05V399/06V410
proposal.description: NHTSA campaigns 05V399 and 06V410 together cover specified 2001-2003 Saab 9-5 V6 vehicles with B308 gasoline engines. The campaign documents describe an ignition-discharge-module IGBT that can overheat and burn out, cause engine stall and increase crash risk; 06V410 expanded the V6 population. Applicability, campaign completion and the installed module version are VIN-specific and must not be inferred from symptoms alone.
proposal.solution: Check the VIN for open campaigns 05V399 and 06V410 and have the authorized recall inspection or module replacement completed if applicable. For a stall, no-start or ignition DTC on a vehicle with completed campaigns, diagnose module power, wiring, engine management and other causes using WIS before replacing parts. Do not buy an ignition discharge module from this page; VIN campaign status, B308 application, bank, installed module and diagnosis determine the remedy.
